sections.title: The City Paradox: Design, Innovation, and Leadership
sections.description: The city is one of the greatest human inventions of the world. Life in urban areas has made us richer, smarter, healthier, and happier. Yet, cities have become sites of some of the meanest and dirtiest jobs, inequity in many forms, and unpredictable violence. The city is a paradox, a laboratory to explore pressing questions about our connected pasts and the fate of our future. Why did Bangalore become a boom town while Detroit declined into oblivion? Is there anything laudable about the slums of Cape Town and Mumbai? Should we celebrate urban sprawl in places like Mexico City, New Delhi, and Beijing? And how do cities with illustrious pasts contend with modern demands? In this course, we will investigate these questions through a comparative history of urban activity around the globe. We shall focus on three interrelated themes: the historical design of cities and the consequences of urban planning; the modern city as a site of accumulation, especially labor, capital, and entrepreneurship; and the social life of cities with attention to how city dwellers, policy leaders, and business innovators fiercely negotiate competing visions of their urban future. The course format combines lecture, discussion, field trips, and guest speakers. Students will also have an opportunity to conduct their own urban ethnography and delve further into a research question about a city’s past or present as part of a required final research paper and presentation.
